summary:
Zamfara was the first Nigerian state to reintroduce Sharia criminal law - its Sharia Establishment Law was introduced on 27 October 1999 and came into force on 27 January 2000 - triggering a cascade of eleven more states by 2002. Hisbah religious-police activity is documented in Zamfara. USCIRF's 2019 implementation study covers Zamfara alongside Kano and Sokoto using 2017 case data, confirming operational Sharia-court function. No trans-specific incident or capital sentence is recorded for Zamfara in this dossier.

Score 0.034 below the national 0.08. The enacted Sharia framework plus Hisbah presence plus USCIRF case evidence justify the deviation. Above Yobe (0.04) by a marginal 0.01: Yobe and Zamfara share the same legal basis and Hisbah documentation; the difference is immaterial and both sit at the lower-Sharia tier. Well above Bauchi (0.02), Kano (0.03), and Sokoto (0.03) where capital-text or capital-sentence evidence is far stronger.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch report (2004) on the extension of Sharia to criminal law in Nigeria: Zamfara's governor was first, introducing the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999 (in force 27 January 2000), and by 2002 twelve northern states had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation - to date the only states where Sharia courts have jurisdiction to try criminal cases.

tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct criminalisation is the adjacent layer here: the federal SSMPA (up to 14 years, applies to tourists) plus the Sharia penal layer for Muslims shape police and Hisbah posture toward any gender-nonconforming presence, even though the written offences target conduct rather than gender identity.
